name: premature-optimization
intent: Records what Premature Optimization costs: effort and structural complexity spent on a performance problem that has not been measured and may not exist, so the code pays the readability, debuggability and maintenance price of the optimisation while still being no faster — and the real bottleneck, elsewhere, is untouched.
problem: A performance concern is acted on before the code exists in a measurable form, so the cost of the optimisation is immediate and attributable while the benefit is speculative. What actually gets optimised is a guess about where time will be spent, and the guess is usually wrong.
context: The canonical framing is Knuth's 1974 statement, which is routinely quoted in a truncated and consequential form: 'We should forget about small efficiencies, say about 97% of the time: premature optimization is the root of all evil. Yet we should not pass up our opportunities in that critical 3%. A good programmer will not be lulled into complacency by such reasoning, he will be wise to look carefully at the critical code; but only after that code has been identified.' Two things are routinely dropped: the 'critical 3%' and the requirement that the critical code be identified first. Wilson's Ubiquity piece makes the second distortion explicit — engineers have extended the maxim to 'you should never optimize your code' and even 'never think about performance until the very end of the cycle', which he argues is a misreading: Hoare said premature optimization, and by 1974 'optimization' meant counting cycles in assembly, which is a different activity from designing performance into a system. His own correction is the practical framing: profile everything, and learn to predict where performance issues will cause problems; choose among otherwise-equivalent constructs the more efficient one, and never give up your performance accidentally.
benefits: It is a decision procedure, not a ban. The full rule is: identify the critical code, then optimize it. The truncated quote destroys the procedure and leaves only the prohibition.

It distinguishes two different activities that share a name: choosing the right algorithm and data structure (which belongs in the design phase and is not premature) versus micro-optimising an implementation you have not measured (which is).
It names the asymmetry honestly — the cost of the optimisation is certain and immediate, the benefit is probabilistic and deferred — which is what makes it the wrong bet under uncertainty.
It is measurable: coverage, a flame graph and a latency budget tell you which code is critical, and 'we have not profiled this' is a checkable statement rather than an opinion.
It is the reason 'choose the more efficient of two otherwise equivalent options' is not premature — that costs nothing in readability and buys performance for free.
tradeoffs: The maxim is contested and has been misused in both directions. softpanorama records that the quote is widely used to argue for bad programming and that Knuth's own 1974 point was pro-optimisation; the acceptance that a 12% improvement, easily obtained, is never marginal in established engineering disciplines is part of the same paper and is routinely dropped.

There are real cases where optimising first is right — a known-bad algorithm on data whose volume is known in advance (an O(n^2) join on a table that will have a billion rows), a hard real-time deadline, a fixed hardware target, or a language/runtime with no escape hatch once shipped.

Deferring everything is also a failure mode. Wilson's argument is that designing without any thought about performance produces systems that rarely perform well even with an extensive optimisation phase at the end, and that the only way to improve them is by rewriting.

'The naive implementation first' is not free: for some code the naive version is structurally impossible to optimise later (a data model that requires a full scan), and the cost of that is discovered at the worst moment.
The 97/3 split is an estimate from 1974 about mainframes and does not transfer to mobile or embedded targets where every millisecond of memory and battery is constrained.
Profiling infrastructure is itself a cost, and for some systems (short-lived scripts, one-off migrations, code executed once) it never pays for itself.
quality_attributes_note: Scores describe the codebase while the smell is present. Performance is the low axis by measurement rather than by construction — the smell means the measured performance is no better than the unoptimised version would have been, while complexity went up. Reliability and security are mid because unreadable code is where defects live, but the smell is a cost and clarity problem rather than a correctness one. Coupling is the one axis that stays healthy, since speculative optimisation is usually local to one function.

participants.responsibility: Acts on an unmeasured performance hypothesis, spending structural complexity on a location chosen by intuition rather than by a profile.
participants.notes: The belief is usually sincere: the requirement was 'fast', and optimising is the visible response to it.

participants.responsibility: The performance expectation that prompted the work — a latency target, a throughput target, or merely an assumption that speed matters here.
participants.notes: Wilson notes that the requirement is often a grey area users only report when the program 'feels too slow' in production.

participants.responsibility: The code that was actually consuming the time or the memory, which the optimisation never touched.
participants.notes: Almost always somewhere else: I/O, a network round trip, an allocation loop, a cache miss, a lock contention point.

participants.responsibility: The measurement that would have identified the critical code before the work was done, and that Knuth's rule requires before the optimisation.
participants.notes: 'Only by timing sections of the program can a programmer learn to predict the performance of similar code segments.'

use_cases: Hand-rolling a balanced tree or a hash index before a single operation has run, on the assumption that the built-in container will be too slow.
Micro-optimising a function called once at startup on the theory that startup matters, with no startup measurement.
Replacing a clear, idiomatic list-based lookup with a precomputed map because 'dictionaries are faster', before the data volume is known.
Introducing a caching layer, an object pool, or a hand-rolled memory arena for code that has never been profiled.
Choosing a lower-level or more complex API (unsafe blocks, raw pointers, hand-rolled serialisation) for a hot path that was assumed rather than measured.
Optimising 'for later' in a prototype whose final shape is unknown, so the optimisation is written against a structure that will not survive.
avoid_when: A performance requirement exists and is written down: a latency budget, a throughput target, a memory ceiling, a battery budget, a hard real-time deadline. With a requirement and a measurement, the optimisation is not premature.
The input volume is known in advance and the current complexity class cannot meet it — an O(n^2) algorithm against a known billion rows is a design decision, not premature optimisation.
The target platform is fixed and unforgiving (embedded, mobile, real-time) and the budget is small enough that the naive approach provably does not fit.

The optimisation is the simpler and clearer option anyway: a dictionary lookup instead of a nested loop, or a single query returning one row instead of filtering a result set in code. Argue about readability; the performance is a bonus.
The language or runtime leaves no room to optimise later — a shipped bytecode artefact, a closed device, or an AOT compilation target where the structure is fixed at build time.
The code has already been profiled and this is the critical section, which is exactly the 3% the full quote describes.
pitfalls: Quoting the truncated version. 'Premature optimization is the root of all evil' without the 3% clause is not what the source says and it produces teams that never think about performance at all.
Treating 'don't optimise prematurely' as 'don't design for performance'. Wilson's argument is that the absence of planned performance is the trunk and the absence of optimisation is a branch.

Optimising the algorithm you are currently writing instead of profiling. The intuition about where the time goes is systematically wrong in systems with I/O, because the bottleneck is rarely the code under consideration.
Micro-optimising in a form the compiler will undo — manual inlining, loop restructuring the optimiser already handles, avoiding the collection methods for no measured reason.
Introducing a cache to solve a problem that was never measured, and inheriting invalidation, staleness and a new failure mode in exchange for speed that was never demonstrated.
Optimising a prototype. The structure of the final code is unknown, so the optimisation is written against something that will not survive, and the complexity survives.
Judging performance by intuition rather than by a baseline: without a measurement before the change, there is no way to know whether it helped.

related_patterns_notes.memoization: Memoization is the safe form: it makes a repeated computation free without changing the algorithm, and its cost is bounded and obvious. Premature optimisation is choosing this before knowing whether the computation repeats or is expensive.
related_patterns_notes.caching: A cache is the premature optimiser's favourite tool, and the reason it is also a reliability pattern is that it introduces invalidation — a correctness problem bought with speed that was never measured.
related_patterns_notes.flyweight: Sharing immutable structure to reduce memory is a legitimate data-oriented choice when memory is a stated constraint, and premature when it is applied because 'objects are expensive' without a measurement.
related_patterns_notes.object-pool: An object pool is the clearest example of an optimisation that moves cost rather than removing it: it trades allocation for a retention scheme and a lifetime problem, and it needs a profile to justify itself.
related_patterns_notes.data-locality: Data layout and locality are the part of performance design that legitimately belongs in the design phase — choosing the right data structure is not premature optimisation, it is the other 3%.
related_patterns_notes.lazy-initialization: Deferring work is an optimisation with a correctness cost (initialisation must then be thread-safe and must not surprise a caller), so it needs a reason; on the critical path it is often the right one.
related_patterns_notes.guard-clause: A guard clause is the rare case where the early-return structure is both clearer and faster, which is the 'choose the more efficient of otherwise-equivalent options' case.

anti_patterns: The unprofiled hand-roll: replacing a library implementation with a faster one on the basis of an article, a benchmark of a different workload, or a colleague's recollection.
Caching added to 'speed things up' before any measurement, introducing invalidation, staleness and a new class of bug in exchange for unproven speed.
Object pooling, arenas or hand-rolled memory management for code whose allocation cost has never been measured.
Micro-optimisations the compiler undoes — manual inlining, replacing a collection method with a raw loop, avoiding higher-order functions for no measured reason.
Choosing an unsafe or low-level API path in the hope it is faster, trading safety for an unverified performance claim.
Optimising a prototype whose final structure is unknown, so the complexity is written against something that will be rewritten.
Complexity added for a performance concern that was never expressed as a requirement, and therefore can never be verified as met.
Taking the maxim literally as 'never optimise', so no performance requirement is ever written and the only tuning happens after a production incident.
Assuming the bottleneck is where the code is being written, when it is almost always at an I/O boundary, a lock, or an allocation site elsewhere.
design_principles: Measure first: profile everything. Only by timing sections of the program can a programmer learn to predict where performance issues will cause problems.
Optimise the critical code, and only after it has been identified — the 3% clause of the rule is the operative half.
Choose among otherwise-equivalent options the more efficient one; that is not premature optimisation, it is free performance.
Never give up performance accidentally: know the cost of the high-level constructs you use, rather than assuming every statement costs the same.
Design for performance, then optimise: the design and optimisation phases are separate, and the maxim applies to the second.
State the requirement: a performance target that is not written down cannot be met, measured, or argued about.
best_practices: Write the performance requirement before the code: latency, throughput, memory, battery, or a deadline. Without it, optimisation is guesswork in both directions.
Establish a baseline before changing anything — a benchmark, a profile, or a field measurement — so 'this is faster' is a claim with evidence attached.
Choose the right algorithm and data structure first; this is design work and belongs in the first 3%, not in the last 97%.
Let the optimizer do the micro-level work and check that it did by reading the generated code for the genuinely hot sections; do not hand-optimise what the compiler already handles.
Profile under realistic conditions — production-like data volume and concurrency — because the bottleneck at ten rows is not the bottleneck at ten million.
Measure after the change, not before only; an optimisation with no after-measurement has not been demonstrated to work.
Keep experimental optimisations on a branch so they can be reverted cheaply, which is the cheapest insurance against a speculative change.
Watch the platforms where the calculus changes: embedded, mobile and real-time targets have budgets where the 1974 estimate does not apply.
Prefer simpler code when two options are equivalent in performance, and say so in review — that is a stronger argument than a citation.
sources: Donald E. Knuth, 'Structured Programming with go to Statements', ACM Computing Surveys, Vol. 6, No. 4, December 1974, p. 268 — the full quotation including 'about 97% of the time' and 'only after that code has been identified', the 'holy grail of efficiency leads to abuse' passage, the 12% observation that an easily obtained improvement is never marginal in established engineering disciplines, and the attribution of the phrase to Tony Hoare.

Wayne A. Wilson, 'The Fallacy of Premature Optimization', ACM Ubiquity, 2002 — Hoare's meaning of 'optimization' in 1974 (counting cycles in assembly), the distortion into 'never optimize your code', the profile-everything prescription, and the distinction between designing performance into a system and optimising an implementation.
Rico Mariani's maxim, cited in Wilson's piece: 'Never give up your performance accidentally' — programmers usually assume every statement costs the same, which is the accidentally-given-up case.
Tony Hoare, who later disclaimed having coined the phrase, attributing it to Knuth — the attribution is genuinely muddled and the full 1974 context was pro-optimisation, not anti-optimisation.
